title: Selrick
mood: At dawn Chang’e takes hold of a coat. Weeks later, on the ruins of the base, two of them start a school.

hero.alt: The sun comes up behind the towers of Terrinia, lighting the whole city gold, a tall tower in its middle sending a thin beam into the sky.
hero.credit: Official Layla and Fanny lore trailer

segs.t: At dawn Chang’e sat on a broken curb at the foot of the avenue, her knees drawn up. Her crescents lay dark on the stones beside her, one short. Mr. Bunny hung at her shoulder, his own size again, his screen dimmed low.
Behind her the iron doors stood open in the seawall. People came out into the gray, blinking. The small girl rode out on her father’s hip. Her eyes were open now.
Lesley stood one step away, her hands at her sides. Soot streaked her coat from collar to hem.
Her eye went over Chang’e the way it went over a street. It stopped at the arm Chang’e had landed on, and stayed there.
She’s checking me for damage,
thought Chang’e.
Like a suit.
Once, at the edge of a crater, Lesley had said she was sorry, and Chang’e had pushed at this same coat with both hands. Lesley did not say it again.
Chang’e’s hand went out, the way it had gone out after two white coats. This coat did not walk away. She took a fistful of it and held on.
“Big Sis.”
Lesley did not pull away. She had not pulled away the first time either, in a corridor, with two small fists in her sleeve.
Then she sat down on the curb beside Chang’e, close, and let the coat stay where it was.
She sat very straight, as if waiting for an order. Chang’e knew which question she was waiting for, and did not ask it.
Later,
she thought.
She’s here now.
Lesley did not offer the answer. Chang’e kept hold of the coat until the sun came up over the water.
The ruins of the base. Weeks later.
The gate hung crooked on one hinge. Lesley had not been through it since the night the base fell.
Chang’e went ahead with Mr. Bunny. Lesley went through.
The storehouse by the water was a black shell. The lab still stood. From its door Lesley walked the old line toward the shelter. At thirty steps the ground fell away.
Grass had grown over the crater’s floor. Chang’e came and stood at its edge beside her. For a while they only looked.
Inside the lab the old frame stood where it always had, beside the test ring. Along the wall stood the suits Chang’e had finished in the years apart, empty.

Days later the Shield’s officers came to see the suits, and the city’s scientists with them. The officer with gray in his beard stood at the front. Chang’e climbed onto a crate between the suits so they could see her.
“These run on aspirant power,” she said. “It comes from the pilot.”
“The Shield sent you soldiers,” said the officer. “Not one of them could lift an arm in those.”
“You sent whoever was free. A suit doesn’t care who’s free.”
“Then what does it care about?”
“What you believe, and how hard. Most grown-ups stopped believing hard a long time ago.” She held up one finger. “That’s a guess. I’ll build something to test it.”
“And if it’s right?”

“Then we find them young, and we teach them. In pairs.” Her eyes went to Lesley and away. “The night the Enders came back, my crescents flew farther than they ever had in the yard. I changed nothing in them. Lesley was at my back.”
Lesley had not known that.
“Hearts that believe in each other become our strength,” said Chang’e.
The oldest of the scientists frowned. “That’s a school. Not a regiment.”
“Yes. Here, where the first light was.”
The officer looked out at the burned yard. “And who keeps the suits running?”
“This little scientist will protect the world!” said Chang’e.
The officers laughed.
Lesley did not. One by one they looked at her, and the laughing stopped.
“What does a child fight with?” asked one of them.
“Imagination,” said Lesley. “That’s her weapon. I only aim it.”
Chang’e chose where the hall would stand. She walked out into the yard with a stake and drove it into the crater’s floor.
She did not say why. Lesley had knelt at its edge once, in the ash. She did not ask.
Then Chang’e built a glove wired to a dial. The dial read aspirant power. She held the glove out to Lesley first.
Lesley put her hand in. The glove hummed and lit. The needle swung hard past the line.
Chang’e looked at the needle, then up at her. “Huh,” she said, and wrote it down.

With the dial, Lesley chose her instructors. She tried only Shield soldiers she had fought beside. Most needles stopped short of the line. She kept the rest. One was a young soldier with a monocle, named Joe.

blocks.caption: Joe, one of Lesley’s first instructors.

media.alt: Design art of Joe as a young man: short brown hair, a monocle over one eye, a gray uniform with a cross strap, and a long blade at his side.

segs.t: Among the scaffolds in the yard, the first of them climbed into a suit. It lifted its arm. Then the other.
Chang’e’s pencil fell out of her fingers. She did not pick it up.
“A soldier can wear it,” she whispered.

For the Science Division’s professors, she went first to the researcher who had given her the big bench. He had never left. Then she called back the rest of her parents’ old team. Over the crater, the hall rose wall by wall.
On a bright morning the old gate stood open on new hinges. New letters over it read SELRICK ACADEMY.
That morning Lesley became the Academy’s Chief Combat Instructor, head of its Combat Division. Chang’e became director of its Science Division.
The two of them stood at the gate with Mr. Bunny. A crowd had come to the fence.

In the yard the instructors climbed into their suits. Wings of light opened at their backs, and they went up one after another. In a line they crossed over the gate and the crowd, then the roofs beyond, and swung toward the water.
Along the fence, people cheered. Beside Lesley, Chang’e tipped her head all the way back to watch.
Light over the yard again,
thought Lesley.
This time it went up.
Years ago two Doctors had waited at this gate for her. She had saluted them.
She turned to Chang’e and saluted.
Chang’e stared up at her. Then she saluted back, with the wrong hand.
Lesley did not correct it.
That night the lab’s new lamps were still burning at midnight. Lesley set a cup of caramel pudding outside its door. She laid the spoon across the lid, square to the edge. She left no note.
At the old bench, Chang’e’s mother had handed that flavor round, one cup each.
Lesley’s own room was down the corridor. It had a cot and one hard chair. She set the chair facing the door.
Selrick Academy. The first intake.
For weeks Lesley had walked the city’s children’s homes with stamped sheets. “Come,” she told the ones she chose, and walked off without waiting for an answer.
Now a queue of children ran the length of the yard, past the new hall and across the old fifty steps. Every one of them was taller than Chang’e.
She sat on a stool behind a table, the glove in front of her and Mr. Bunny at her shoulder. Lesley stood at the wall behind her with her rifle on her back.
“Hand in the glove,” said Chang’e. “I’m Chang’e. I read the needle. Lesley asks the questions.”
By noon it came out as one word.
Hand after hand went into the glove. At its hum some came straight back out.
“Name,” said Lesley, to every one of them. “Why are you here?”
Chang’e read the needles. Lesley watched each face while it answered, and let every answer run to its end.

Then she tipped her head at a door. Past the line meant the far one, to the Combat Division’s preparatory course. Short of it meant the left one, to the Support Division. No name went on a list before the queue was done.
One boy ran back toward the gate before his needle had settled. Lesley watched him all the way out.
“I didn’t get his reading,” said Chang’e.
“You got it.”
All down the queue, feet shuffled on the stones.
Dad would have had the count by now,
thought Chang’e.
She read the next needle.
Halfway down the queue came a girl with pink-red twin-tails. Her sheet listed a long line of scientists. She put her hand in the glove, and the needle hit the stop with a click.
The girl answered Lesley without slowing and walked on to the far door. She never once looked back to see who was behind her.
When the yard was empty at last, Chang’e went back through the sheets.
“Best reading of the day,” she said.
“She doesn’t look back,” said Lesley.
“Is that bad?”
“In a pair it is.”
Chang’e tapped the sheet. “We’re taking her.”
“We’re taking her,” said Lesley.
That night the lists came up on Chang’e’s screen in the lab. Lesley read over her shoulder.
The Combat Division’s first intake ran down in a column. Layla. Guinevere of House Baroque. Vexana. The rest.
Lesley read every name twice, then looked at the empty screen below the last one.
“If only you’d had a proper instructor...” she said, low.
Chang’e looked up. “Who?”
“Nobody.” Lesley straightened. “Rounds.” She went out.
Chang’e scrolled down to the Science Division’s list. Near its end was a face she had been looking for: the girl from the salvage stall.
Beside the face was a name.
Selena.

The week before the entry, Chang’e had stopped at a trestle table at the city’s edge. On its corner an old servo turned its arm back and forth. Under the soot on its label tape was her mother’s small quick hand. Someone had mended it with a trick Chang’e had never seen.
“Hands,” the girl had said, when Chang’e asked with what.
Chang’e had paid every coin in her pockets for it, and two jelly candies. It stood on the shelf above the bench now, still turning its arm.
On the screen, the family-name box beside Selena’s name was empty. It glowed red.
No family,
thought Chang’e.
The city’s full of children like that.
She had never asked who her own first parents were.
She laid her thumb on the box. The red cleared, and the box went green.
On the bench the photograph lay face down, as it had since the night of the fall. Chang’e set it on her desk, face up, and left it there.
Lesley’s room. Dawn.
In the hard chair, Lesley opened her eye. The window had gone gray.
The rifle still lay across her knees, its bolt drawn back. On the cot lay the new coil, where Chang’e had set it yesterday.
She took it up and fitted it on top of the old action.
Down the corridor, the lab light was still on.
